item.title: NeuroLens: Learning Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics from Chronic Recordings
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Hanrui Lyu, Baiyuan Chen, Tianshu Tan, Matthew R. Whiteway, Maxwell D. Melin, Ji Xia, Linyang He, Bradly C. Stadie, Anne Churchland, Liam Paninski, Yizi Zhang
arXiv:2610.02864v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how neural activity represents higher-order cognition and how these representations evolve during learning is a central pursuit in neuroscience. However, tracking meaningful representational changes remains challenging because recorded neural populations change across days. Here, we introduce NeuroLens (Latent Embeddings of Neural Semantics), a self-supervised model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (LeJEPA). An adaptive encoder maps changing neural populations into a common latent space, where a temporal predictor forecasts future latent states. Across mouse and human intracortical recordings, NeuroLens learns representations that improve decoding of abstract variables, including decisions and sentence meaning. In chronic mouse neural recordings during visual decision-making, these representations capture gradual transitions between learning stages and the progressive orthogonalization of neural states associated with different choices. They also reveal distinct timescales of cortical reorganization across tasks during learning. With multi-day pretraining, these representations also support stable decoding across days, including leading performance on the FALCON benchmark. Together, these findings support NeuroLens as a framework for tracking learning-related representational changes while maintaining stable decoding over long timescales.

item.title: History-bearing thalamocortical signals reconstruct and redirect later decisions in a circuit model
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Yanzhe Zhao, Yongzhang Ji
arXiv:2611.28799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experience can guide an ambiguous choice or bias a choice despite strong current evidence. We asked how a thalamocortical circuit carries historical content forward and regulates its influence across successive decisions. In published data from adult male mice, suppressing posterior parietal cortex (PPC) or pulvinar (PUL) improved current judgments most when sensory history conflicted with the stimulus, reflecting reduced historical weighting. In trained thalamocortical circuit models, replaying recorded PUL input to PPC reconstructed a historical trace after equalizing complete recipient states across histories. Replaying the opposite history redirected the later choice, even after the circuit correctly judged an intervening strong stimulus. This historical message occupied a low-dimensional direction in thalamic output that remained broadly reachable under firing-rate bounds; redistributing the arriving current at matched energy showed that fine spatial organization, beyond total input strength, selectively shapes later history use without disrupting current choices. Strong sensory evidence suppressed historical output while preserving internal state differences, whereas ambiguity recruited neuronal rectification thresholds and readout alignment to express history. Small shifts in the cortical operating point modulated later historical influence, and partial attenuation of recurrent drive reduced it across all circuits while preserving current commitments; correspondingly, recurrent dynamics were essential for predicting post-stimulus trajectories in held-out histories. Together, these findings distinguish three operations in history-guided choice: returning thalamocortical input determines which past is reconstructed, recurrent dynamics carry its influence forward across intervening demands, and current sensory evidence gates how strongly it enters the decision.

item.title: Shared and context-dependent cortico-striatal-cerebellar organization of temporal prediction
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Pinho, A. L., Koranteng-Addo, V., Alsibaie, A., Patel, N., Diedrichsen, J., Grahn, J. A.
Temporal prediction is thought to draw on two subcortical structures: the basal ganglia for the periodic beat, and the cerebellum for the aperiodic interval. Lesion, imaging and electrophysiological studies converge on this division, yet each tests it within a single modality and task, leaving its generality unknown. We developed a battery of timing tasks for multi-task fMRI, densely sampling 31 non-clinical adults in every combination of temporal structure, sensory modality and task. Encoding engaged the same cortico-striatal-cerebellar architecture throughout. Within it, the dorsal striatum was uniquely selective for the production task. Pooled across tasks, it responded more to auditory beat than interval sequences, whereas the cerebellum did not distinguish them. Yet, removing regularity did not lower that response: the preference is for the beat, not for predictability. Temporal prediction therefore draws on a shared architecture whose striatal node is context-dependent: tuned to periodic time, and to time turned into action.

item.title: From joint attention to shared symbols: A free-energy principle account
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Tadahiro Taniguchi, Koji Hashimoto, Ryuichiro Ishikawa
arXiv:2611.30788v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Joint attention precedes vocabulary acquisition. How can attending to the same object help two people with different sensory experiences come to use a shared word? In a free-energy principle account, marginalizing the common object induces a statistical dependence between private perceptual states. In a categorical world, the joint prior inherits a mixture structure whose component index provides a candidate for shared reference. The collective predictive coding model approximates this prior by representing the dependence through that shared index. An established Metropolis-Hastings naming game lets agents infer and exchange words using private evidence. Toy and multiview image experiments illustrate how word exchange can coordinate private categories and improve the fit of collective models. The account connects joint attention to shared symbols through the coupling of private inference.

item.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wang, Q., Guo, Y., Nie, W., Yang, Q., Zhang, S., Luo, C., Zhang, Y., Zuo, X.-N.
Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

item.title: How Do Large Language Models Learn Concepts During Continual Pre-Training?
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Barry Menglong Yao (UC Davis), Sha Li (Virginia Tech), Yunzhi Yao (UCLA), Minqian Liu (Virginia Tech), Zaishuo Xia (UC Davis), Qifan Wang (Meta AI), Lifu Huang (UC Davis)
arXiv:2601.03570v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human beings primarily understand the world through concepts (e.g., dog), abstract mental representations that structure perception, reasoning, and learning. However, how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and forget such concepts during continual pretraining remains poorly understood. In this work, we study how individual concepts are acquired and forgotten, as well as how multiple concepts interact through interference and synergy. We link these behavioral dynamics to LLMs' internal concept circuits, computational subgraphs associated with specific concepts, and incorporate graph metrics to characterize circuit topology. Our analysis reveals: (1) LLMs' concept circuits provide a non-trivial, consistent signal of concept learning and forgetting; (2) concept circuit topology evolves stage-wise, rising during concept acquisition, and transiently rising before declining during concept forgetting; (3) semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones; (4) conceptual knowledge differs in their transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others. Together, our findings provide a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and motivate concept-aware training strategies, such as Circuit-aware Experience Replay, which uses circuit topology to prioritize concepts vulnerable to forgetting.

item.title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Yuxiang Wei, Zundong Wu, Weiyu Sun, Qizhen Lan, Yanteng Zhang, Vince D. Calhoun
arXiv:2611.28508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

item.title: DiRGeo: Learning Directional Geometry of Visual Representations
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Muhammad Ahtesham, Xin Zhong
arXiv:2611.29057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional geometric measures of visual representations are symmetric, assigning equal costs to forward and reverse motion along the same path. We propose DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over frozen visual representations. Grounded in Randers geometry, DiRGeo learns a state-dependent directional field from ordered image trajectories through self-supervised contrast, without semantic labels. Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition distinguish learned directional structure from normalization artifacts and common convergence. Experiments across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple representation depths demonstrate consistent directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry beyond simple attractor-based explanations. The learned fields become increasingly process-specific in deeper representations, while natural-video experiments reveal event-dependent directional preferences. As functional validation, DiRGeo guides restoration selection. These results establish directional geometry as a useful complement to symmetric representation analysis.

item.title: Do VLMs Align Better with Humans than LLMs Do during Natural Reading?
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Jinzhou Wu, Zhengwu Ma, Jixing Li, Baoping Tang, Zitong Lu
arXiv:2605.28818v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly useful computational models of human language processing, yet it remains open whether vision--language learning is associated with more human-like text representations during natural reading. We address this question by comparing matched LLM and vision--language model (VLM) pairs under strictly text-only input and evaluating alignment with human brain activity (whole-cortex fMRI) and reading behavior (synchronized regressive saccades). Across evaluated pairs, we identify a selective, rather than global, pattern in human--model alignment. In first-party continued-pretraining pairs (Qwen2 and DeepSeek), VLMs more accurately predicted human regressive saccades while exhibiting practical equivalence with matched LLMs in whole-cortex fMRI alignment, whereas a LoRA-adapted pair (Mistral/Idefics2) showed no divergence. However, sentence-level fMRI analyses revealed a growing VLM advantage for more visually evocative sentences. Together, these findings provide a controlled comparison of matched LLMs and VLMs, showing selective human-alignment advantages in reading behavior and visually grounded content.

item.title: From Clever Hans to Hypotheses: Interpreting EEG Foundational Transformers with LRP
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Justus Meyer zu Bexten, Nico Scherf, Bogdan Franczyk, Simon M. Hofmann
arXiv:2605.11885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Emerging foundation models (FMs) in electroencephalography (EEG) promise a path to scale deep learning in diagnostics and brain-computer interfaces despite data scarcity, yet their opaque nature remains a barrier to wider adoption. We investigate attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) as a post-hoc attribution method for EEG-FMs, extending LRP's use on convolutional neural network (CNN)-based EEG models to the Transformer architectures that current FMs are based on. We find that LRP can both verify EEG-FM decisions and surface novel, biologically plausible hypotheses from them. In motor imagery, it unmasks 'Clever Hans' behavior where models prioritize task correlated ocular signals over the intended motor correlates. In a naturalistic paradigm for affect prediction, it reveals a recurring reliance on a central electrode cluster, suggesting a candidate sensorimotor signature of arousal. Though heatmap interpretation remains ambiguous in this complex domain, the results position LRP as a tool for both verification and exploration of EEG-FMs, a role that will grow in both importance and discovery potential as the underlying models mature.

item.title: Cognitive Load modulates the exploration-exploitation trade-off Through Reconfiguration of an IPS-Centered Decision Network
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Dai, H., Wang, L., Yin, X., Liang, X., Ying, Y., Zeng, Y., Niu, L., Roiser, J., Tan, X., Zhang, R.
In dynamic environments where rewards continuously change, adaptive decision-making requires ongoing updates of option-value and uncertainty estimates to balance exploration and exploitation. This process depends on cognitive resources and involves coordinated interactions among multiple brain regions; however, how cognitive load affects directed exploration in such dynamic environments, and whether these effects are accompanied by changes in interactions among exploration-related brain regions, remains unclear. We embedded a working-memory load manipulation within a dynamic four-armed bandit task. Experiment 1 compared computational models and quantified load-related changes in exploration; Experiment 2 examined these behavioral effects in an independent sample and investigated their neural correlates using fMRI. Across both experiments, high load reduced the uncertainty bonus parameter ({varphi}), indicating weaker directed exploration. Experiment 2 additionally showed lower inverse temperature ({beta}) under high load, indicating more stochastic choices. Directed exploration relative to exploitation more activated the frontopolar cortex (FP), intraparietal sulcus (IPS), anterior insula (aIns), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC). Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analyses indicated stronger functional coupling between the right aIns and IPS under low load. Guided by the candidate connections identified by PPI, dynamic causal modeling (DCM) focused on a three-region subnetwork. Bayesian model selection favored the model with directed-exploration-related input to the IPS, while condition-specific comparisons suggested stronger aIns-to-IPS effective connectivity under low load. Together, these findings link cognitive resource demands to reduced uncertainty-guided directed exploration in a dynamic environment and suggest that this behavioral change is accompanied by selective reconfiguration of interactions within an IPS-centered decision subnetwork.

item.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Temudo, A., Nicolas, J., King, B. R., Albouy, G.
Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

item.title: Pretraining Representation Lottery Determines Fine-tuning Generalization
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Fuming Yang, Core Francisco Park
arXiv:2611.28777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large scale pretraining (PT) followed by fine-tuning (FT) is the central paradigm of modern deep learning, yet how PT shapes FT generalization remains poorly understood. We use a synthetic setup in which the ground-truth concept geometry of entities is known, as a controlled testbed to study how representational geometry affects model behavior and how PT representations determine FT generalization. We first show that models differing only in training seed can closely match in PT loss yet vary substantially in FT generalization. We hypothesize that a representational lottery underlies this phenomenon: the random seed dependent geometry formed during PT determines what FT can reach. We confirm this causally. First, injecting the ground-truth concept geometry into the model yields near-ceiling FT generalization, showing that good representations directly drive generalization. Then, distilling a lucky seed's learned representation into an unlucky seed unlocks FT generalization, while distilling the same model's behavior does not. Furthermore, representation distillation can merge entities that never interacted during PT, which FT alone cannot. Finally, we show that regularizing representational drift during FT enables naturalistic learning: only models with good representations learn the task, and they generalize, while models with poor representations fail to fit it. Under plain FT, by contrast, models with poor representations fit the training objective by reshaping their pretrained representations. We reproduce the distillation result in Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, each pretrained multiple times with different random seeds, and show that the transferable representation lives in the deep layers at both scales. Overall, PT acts as a lottery over representations, and the representation a model draws determines how it adapts during FT in a way that behavior alone does not explain.

item.title: Subjective functions
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Samuel J. Gershman
arXiv:2512.15948v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Where do objective functions come from? How do we select what goals to pursue? Human intelligence is adept at synthesizing new objective functions on the fly. How does this work, and can we endow artificial systems with the same ability? This paper proposes an approach to answering these questions, starting with the concept of a subjective function, a higher-order objective function that is endogenous to the agent (i.e., defined with respect to the agent's features, rather than an external task). Expected prediction error is studied as a concrete example of a subjective function. This proposal has many connections to ideas in psychology, neuroscience, and machine learning.

item.title: A generative framework for unified representations bridging electrophysiological and haemodynamic brain activity
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Weiheng Yao, Changhong Jing, Xuhang Chen, Chi-Man Pun, Michael Kwok-Po Ng, Shuqiang Wang
arXiv:2611.28507v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electrophysiological and haemodynamic recordings resolve brain activity at complementary temporal and spatial scales, yet paired acquisition remains difficult to scale. We propose a generative framework that aligns paired multimodal recordings in a unified representation space and generates modality-specific haemodynamic responses from EEG. In paired cohorts, the framework generated fMRI BOLD and fNIRS haemoglobin responses that reproduced regional dynamics, cortical maps, functional connectivity and task structure. Generated BOLD followed Real BOLD time courses and cortical patterns, while Generated haemoglobin responses tracked task-evoked HbO and HbR dynamics. The framework enabled decoding across visual, motor-imagery and mental-arithmetic tasks, independent-record decoding, external BOLD localization and low-sample augmentation. Paired feature-space calibration supported bidirectional retrieval. The proposed framework extends cortical analysis and brain decoding to EEG recordings when Real haemodynamic data are sparse.

item.title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Chenhao Zhang
arXiv:2611.28665v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

item.title: Beyond Forgetting: Representation Misdirection Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Tien Dang, The-Hai Nguyen, Dinh Mai Phuong, Nguyen Minh Phuong, Anh Bui, Hoang Thanh-Tung, Le-Minh Nguyen, Naoya Inoue
arXiv:2601.21702v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider Representation Misdirection (RM), a simple unlearning mechanism for large language models (LLMs) that achieves unlearning by redirecting the latent representations of forget samples toward a target vector. Despite being important, the role of the target vector used in RM remains insufficiently explored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH). Specifically, if one can identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the LRH enables linear operations on this concept vector within the representation space of the forget samples. From this perspective, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning via RM elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. We empirically validate this hypothesis across a wide range of concepts and tasks, including controlling unlearned models' truthfulness, sentiment, stereotypical bias, refusal, language, and instruction-following. Our findings reveal that this phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing unlearned models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

item.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Muxin Fu, Peike Yu, Guibin Zhang, Wenrui Zhou, Runze Liu, Lang Feng, Fuchao Yang, Feng Chen, Yixuan Li, Mengao Zhang, Shiying Zhang, Wen Shen, Ling Pan, Shuicheng Yan, Bo An
arXiv:2611.28649v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

item.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Stanislav, B. T., Mangnus, M., Stehr, D., Lewis, A. G., Hagoort, P., Basnakova, J., Stolk, A.
Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.

item.title: Age and bilingual language experience are associated with large-scale functional network reorganization
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: SocArXiv
Michal Korenar et al.
Aging is associated with changes in large-scale functional brain organization, such as reductions in network segregation, which have been interpreted as a feature of age-related neural dedifferentiation. However, functional network organization may may also reflect accumulated life experiences. Bilingualism, in particular, has been linked to experience-dependent variation in cognitive and neural systems supporting language processing and executive control. Whether bilingualism is associated with network segregation across adulthood, and how these associations vary with language experience, remains unclear. To address this question, the present multisite study examines resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) among the Language network, the Default Mode (DMN), and the Multiple Demand (MD) (which support language processing, internally directed cognition, and domain-general cognitive control, respectively). The sample comprised N= 605 adults spanning younger to older adulthood, drawn from eight independent datasets across four sociolinguistic contexts. Older age was associated with less segregation across all three network pairs. Notably, bilingual adults showed greater Language–DMN, Language–MD, and DMN–MD segregation than monolingual adults. Immersion-defined contrasts further revealed variation across linguistic environments such that both immersed and non-immersed bilinguals showed greater DMN-MD segregation than monolinguals, while greater Language–MD segregation was observed primarily in immersed bilinguals compared to monolinguals. In contrast, continuous measures of bilingual experience were not significantly associated with segregation and did not modulate age-related differences. Together, these findings highlight age-related reductions in network segregation and demonstrate that bilingual language experience is associated with systemic differences in large-scale functional network organization across adulthood.

item.title: Do infants and toddlers seek to resolve their uncertainty-induced curiosity?
item.description:
Relevance: 24% | Source: SocArXiv
Hambel Willow et al.
Curiosity and information-seeking behaviours occur from early childhood, with infants demonstrating multiple exploratory behaviours (Bazhydai & Westermann, 2019), for example, when encountering new objects in their environment and attempting to learn more about them. Infants' and toddlers' curiosity helps them navigate the world, particularly when developing new knowledge and understanding (Jirout et al., 2024). This links with infants’ novelty orienting (Sokolov, 1963 cited in Twomey & Westermann, 2018) and broad exploration (Lee et al. 2023), which drives their early learning and development. Previous work has examined adults’ epistemic curiosity (seeking specific information in response to uncertainty) by presenting them with a blurred image and then giving them a choice: to press a button to reveal the clear resolution of the previously blurred image (reducing their uncertainty) or press another button to see a clear new image (Nicki, 1970). Findings revealed that adults sought to resolve their curiosity, as they chose to see the clear resolution of the previously blurred images significantly more often than the clear novel images. However, these curiosity resolution behaviours were not replicated in infancy research, with findings revealing no significant difference in 8-month-olds’ fixations between clear resolution and clear novel images after being presented with a blurred image (Chen et al., 2022). In this study, however, there was a potential conflict, as the clear resolution and clear novel images were presented side-by-side simultaneously on screen. Therefore, infants’ seeking to resolve curiosity could have competed with their novelty preference, which could explain the null findings. Based on these findings, a key question remains: when infants and toddlers have an explicit choice, do they seek to resolve their curiosity or engage with novelty? The current eye-tracking study builds on the work of Chen et al. (2022) by presenting infants (aged 8-10-months) and toddlers (aged 22-24-months) with a blurred image on screen and then giving them a choice, using a gaze-contingent paradigm, to either see the clear resolution of the previously blurred image or a clear novel image. Gaze contingency was deemed appropriate as it has been used in previous research with both infants (Wang et al., 2012) and toddlers (Poli et al., 2024). The study also includes a control condition, where children see a clear image first and then have a choice to see the blurred version of this image or a new blurred image. This control condition is implemented to investigate if preference for a related image is driven by perceptual overlap rather than the drive to resolve uncertainty. We are also interested in whether children’s looking preferences are affected by their trait curiosity. Trait curiosity is measured using the Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (Altmann et al., 2025) designed for children aged 5-24-months. We are using this questionnaire alongside the eye tracking data as it gives an indication of children's curiosity in their daily lives, with the questionnaire covering many curiosity behaviours in early childhood including interacting with stimuli in the environment, enjoying exposure to novel stimuli and attempting to learn new information. For the current study we are focusing on Sensory-type curiosity (associated with enjoying exposure to novel stimuli) and Investigative-type curiosity (associated with seeking to resolve uncertainty). We hypothesise that first, toddlers will seek to resolve curiosity significantly more frequently than infants, who will demonstrate a stronger novelty preference. Second, we predict that toddlers will have significantly shorter latency for triggering the resolution images and novel images compared to infants. Third, we predict that infants will fixate at the novel images significantly more than toddlers. Finally, we predict an influence of trait curiosity on these behaviours, with infants and toddlers scoring higher on Investigative-type curiosity seeking to resolve curiosity significantly more, whereas those scoring higher on Sensory-type curiosity having a stronger novelty preference. We will measure children’s choice ratio for triggering the resolution compared to the novel images; the latency for triggering the resolution compared to the novel images; the fixation times for the resolution compared to the novel images, and the influence of trait curiosity on these preferential looking behaviours. The results of this study will illustrate the development of curiosity-based exploration in infancy and toddlerhood, the relationship between resolving curiosity and experiencing novelty within these early age groups, and how trait curiosity shapes visual exploration behaviours.

item.title: Music-Based Interventions for Cognition and Brain Health: the ARM framework
item.description:
Relevance: 24% | Source: SocArXiv
Psyche Loui et al.
Music-based interventions (MBIs) have shown promise in addressing cognitive, motor, and language impairments across neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions. Despite an increasing number of controlled studies that have assessed the potential rehabilitative effects of music, neural mechanisms underlying therapeutic benefits remain poorly understood. Here we present the ARM framework: a neurobiologically-informed model integrating three key systems: Auditory processing networks that encode temporal and spectral features; Reward circuitry activated by musical pleasure and prediction, and Motor systems engaged through auditory-motor coupling and rhythmic entrainment. We examine how specific MBIs leverage these systems to varying degrees and show how understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting individual treatment response, personalizing interventions, and developing next-generation therapeutic approaches that optimize engagement of specific neural systems.
